newsitem.title: USA: Dayton Hudson expects gains at Mervyn's.
newsitem.headline: Dayton Hudson expects gains at Mervyn's.

text.p: Dayton Hudson Corp said Tuesday its troubled Mervyn's division would post sales gains by the end of the year.

Dayton Hudson, parent of Target discount stores and Marshall Field's department stores, has been struggling to mend the Mervyn's chain for several years. Deep cost cuts and fewer merchandise markdowns put profits on the upswing last year, but sales have been stubbornly weak.
"Clearly we expect a return to positive comparable-store sales this year," said Dayton Hudson's chief financial officer, Douglas Scovanner, in an interview.
"I think there's a whole lot more that's going right than wrong at Mervyn's."

That wasn't always the case. Two years ago, the Minneapolis-based company plunged into a drive to overhaul Mervyn's, revamping its offerings to include more name-brand merchandise, slashing expenses by $100 million in 1996, exiting non-strategic markets in Florida and Georgia and shaking up management.

The moves have helped lift the Mervyn's bottomline. In 1996, Mervyn's operating profits rose 50 percent to $153 million. And earlier Tuesday, Dayton Hudson reported Mervyn's operating profit rose 30 percent to $51 million during the first quarter.

But sales at the 276-store chain, which accounts for about one-fifth of the company's total revenues, were disappointing, the company said. Same-store sales, or sales at stores open a year, were flat during the quarter.

"Clearly Mervyn's was not up to our plan," Scovanner said. He said the company was still "fine-tuning" Mervyn's strategy and expected same-store sales to rise by the low-single-digits in percentage terms this year.
Industry experts said Dayton Hudson faced heavy pressure to fix Mervyn's sales because future profit growth would be hard to come by without it, unless it can find more expenses to trim.
"What they need to do now is strike a balance between modest sales growth and improved gross margin," said Wayne Hood of Prudential Securities.

Although the company says it is pleased with progress Mervyn's has made in improving profits, it recently named a new executive, Bart Butzer, a former regional manager at Target, to replace Paul Sauser as president of Mervyn's.
A Mervyn's spokeswoman said the change was by mutual decision by the company and Sauser, but analysts said it likely reflected disappointment with Mervyn's sales.
Dayton Hudson does not expect to shed more Mervyn's stores beyond its decision to retreat from Florida and Georgia and to close or sell 10 underperforming units, Scovanner said.

For now shareholders were applauding Dayton Hudson's handling of Mervyn's, Scovanner said. The company's shares have climbed far above the offer of $90 to $95 a share it received last year from J.C. Penney Co Inc, one of Mervyn's chief rivals, to about $147 a share on a pre-split basis.
"I think that on balance shareholders are satisfied with the return that they've enjoyed during our period of intense focus on Mervyn's performance," he said.
